strengths: Establishes a rigorous theoretical foundation for Cartesian equivariant models by introducing Cartesian-3j symbols and Cartesian Generalized Clebsch-Gordan Coefficients.

Conducts the first controlled, architecture-fixed comparison between spherical and Cartesian representations (cNequIP, cAllegro, cMACE), proving that irreducible Cartesian models can reach comparable accuracy to their spherical counterparts.
Provides valuable practical insights and design principles (e.g., avoiding Cartesian-3j at the edge level) to mitigate the unfavorable compute and memory scaling inherent in Cartesian models.

Demonstrates strong empirical performance on the Matbench Discovery benchmark with the proposed TACE-v1-OAM-M model, achieving competitive F1 scores and state-of-the-art level thermal conductivity predictions.
weaknesses: Irreducible Cartesian tensors suffer from exponential growth in dimensions at higher ranks, making higher truncations (e.g., rank 4 or above) practically infeasible with the current implementation.

Unlike spherical tensor libraries that benefit from specialized GPU acceleration libraries (such as cuEquivariance or oeq), the pure PyTorch implementation of this Cartesian framework leads to higher memory footprints and Out-Of-Memory (OOM) issues on larger systems.

The presentation in Section 4.1 concerning the Cartesian-3j symbols and the relationship between Equation 5 and Equation 11 is mathematically dense and would benefit from clearer notation and more intuitive explanation of the basis transformations.

strengths: Establishes a rigorous mathematical framework for irreducible Cartesian tensors (ICTs) by introducing Cartesian-3j symbols and Cartesian Generalized Clebsch-Gordan coefficients.
Provides the first controlled, 'head-to-head' comparison between spherical and Cartesian representations under fixed model architectures (NequIP, Allegro, MACE) on the 3BPA dataset.

Shows strong empirical validation on a large-scale benchmark (Matbench Discovery) with the proposed TACE-v1-OAM-M model, demonstrating competitive accuracy compared to state-of-the-art spherical potentials.
Open-sources the extended library ('cartnn') to support irreducible Cartesian tensor products and contractions, aiding community reproducibility.
weaknesses: The Cartesian approach suffers from a severe dimensionality curse, leading to unfavorable compute and memory scaling (including multiple OOM instances as rank increases) compared to spherical tensors.

The Cartesian models do not show any significant accuracy improvement over their spherical counterparts, making the practical motivation for adopting this computationally heavier framework somewhat weak.

The explanation of how tensor contractions decompose into irreducible components (Section 4.3 and Table 7) relies heavily on empirical observations rather than a generalized, closed-form theoretical proof.

strengths: Establishes a solid theoretical foundation for irreducible Cartesian tensor operations by introducing Cartesian-3j symbols and Cartesian Generalized Clebsch-Gordan Coefficients.
Enables the first truly controlled comparison between spherical and Cartesian representations by keeping the neural architectures (NequIP, Allegro, MACE) fixed and varying only the tensor basis.

Provides highly valuable practical insights and design principles for building efficient Cartesian models (e.g., performing contractions at the edge level and projections at the node level to save memory).

TACE-v1-OAM-M achieves competitive performance on the Matbench Discovery benchmark, especially in the thermal conductivity metric which relies on higher-order derivatives of the potential energy surface.
weaknesses: The Cartesian representation exhibits unfavorable memory and computational scaling as the tensor rank increases, limiting its practical throughput compared to highly optimized spherical counterparts with specialized GPU kernels (such as cuEquivariance).
The implementation of the Irreducible Cartesian Tensor Contraction (ICTC) is not fully integrated into the e3nn wrapper, which somewhat limits the completeness of the released library.
